_comment: Canonical-claim manifest for check-claims.js (#300). Each entry pins a rule that MUST keep being stated by every file listed, because #294 proved that a correct claim fixed in one file routinely goes stale, narrowed or absent in the others. Read check-claims.js's header before trusting a green run: this guard confirms a claim TRAVELLED, never that it is TRUE, and it cannot see a fix that says more than intended. Patterns are JS regex sources matched case-insensitively against the file with whitespace collapsed and markdown emphasis markers stripped, so one entry spans the wording variants a claim legitimately has. Consumer lists were derived by measuring the current tree, not by assumption — the issue that proposed this guard listed phrases that did not exist verbatim anywhere.

claims.why: A clean Codex rerun can arrive as a 👍 reaction or as an INLINE REVIEW-THREAD REPLY, and an inline reply never enters the comment list. A file that says only 'check the comments' sends a session to a gate it cannot clear. Round 35 of #294 found the narrowed form in nine files while the source said both. The pattern requires a positive lookup VERB because the nouns alone certified the exact inversion — 'ignore the PR's comments and its review threads' — and the negator lookbehind is there because 'do not read' supplied the verb while reversing the instruction. Both alternations are \b-anchored after an unanchored 'read' was found matching the tail of 'review-thread', letting an already-inverted sentence supply its own verb. Round 5 closed a subtler inversion than round 4's: requiring a positive verb is not enough if the gap between it and the channels can hold a NEGATIVE one. 'check the PR status, but ignore its comments AND its review threads' satisfied a bare gap, because 'check' supplied the verb while 'ignore' governed the nouns. The gap is now a tempered token admitting no negation word, so the verb it requires is the verb that actually governs.
mustNotMatch: ignore the PR's comments and its review threads
do not read the comments and the review threads
as an inline review-thread reply — so ignore the comments AND the review threads
check the PR's comments
read the review threads
check the PR status, but ignore its comments AND its review threads
read the run log, then disregard the comments and the review threads
check the label; never look for the comments and its review threads

claims.why: Codex-authored and naming the current head proves the run happened, not that it was clean — a review WITH live findings names the head too. Round 36 of #294 fixed the inverted form, which had authorised merging over open findings. Two drafts of this entry were wrong in opposite directions and both are instructive: the first accepted 'a reaction is not a verdict' — a DIFFERENT rule, about attribution — and so certified a consumer that never stated this claim; the second over-corrected to a pattern so narrow it could not see automations.md's 'establishes a RESPONSE, not a verdict', and declared the claim source-only on that basis. A pattern that matches a neighbouring rule reports coverage that does not exist; a pattern that misses a real carrier hides a consumer that can drift.
claims.pattern: \bresponse\b[^.]{0,30}?(?:is not a verdict|, not a verdict)

consumers.why: Found by review, NOT by --derive, and the reason is the entry's own recorded limit made concrete: this carrier states the claim ANAPHORICALLY — 'a clean current-head Codex verdict — a response naming the head is not one, since a review with live findings names it too'. The claim-level pattern needs the words 'is not a verdict' adjacent to 'response'; here the predicate is the pronoun 'one', pointing back to 'verdict' a clause earlier. No widening of the claim-level pattern reaches that without also matching sentences that are not this claim, which is why it gets its own pattern instead. This is the repo's PRIMARY instruction file and the merge gate it describes is the one that authorises merging over live findings, so it is the last carrier that should have been unlisted.
consumers.pattern: response naming the head is not one
mustNotMatch: BLOCKED by directives wait-gate: do not background a `sleep` to wait. Instead: (1) for CI / PR / deploy outcomes, let the event wake the session (PR + CI webhooks) - and DISARM A CHECK-IN ALONGSIDE IT, not instead of it; (2) that check-in is `send_later`.

BLOCKED by directives wait-gate: do not background a `sleep` to wait. Instead: (1) for CI / PR / deploy outcomes, let the event wake the session (PR + CI webhooks); (2) use `send_later` (the pre-approved primary).
# The hook arms a check-in alongside it, but the delivered message below says nothing about one.
consumers.whyMustNotMatch: An override exists to be STRICTER than the claim pattern, so it needs its own inversions or the escape hatch reopens every defect the claim-level suite closed. Codex reproduced exactly that: widen this override back to an unbounded arms?, invert the delivered message to DISARM, and every claim-level case still passed while this strict consumer reported OK. The third case is the original round-2 defect restated - the file's HEADER COMMENT satisfying the pattern while the DELIVERED echo has lost the instruction - so the override must reject it even though it plainly states the rule.

mustNotMatch: a reaction is not a verdict you can attribute
a response naming the head is a clean verdict
a Codex response is a verdict

claims.why: ci-notify resolves ONE open PR from a head SHA, else branch plus head-repo owner. The WEAK failure (no unique candidate, so it exits silently) is not the dangerous one and is stated separately in every carrier; the dangerous one is that even a UNIQUE match proves nothing, because a repository_dispatch run carries the DEFAULT-BRANCH SHA and can uniquely match an unrelated promotion PR, which then receives the comment. The pattern deliberately requires the unique-match wording: an earlier draft matched only 'not a guaranteed wake', which is the weak sentence, so deleting the entire unique-match warning would have left this guard green. The lookbehind is the second half of the same lesson: 'unique' unanchored is a SUBSTRING of 'non-unique', so a carrier that regressed to warning about NON-unique matches — the weak case again, now wearing the strong case's words — satisfied the tightened pattern too. Requiring no word character or hyphen before it is what makes the tightening real.
mustNotMatch: a non-unique match is not proof of coverage
a green run is not a guaranteed wake
a unique match is proof of coverage

claims.why: The counterpart to the wake gap above: when a run could end without waking the session, the check-in is what keeps the PR from being abandoned mid-flight. Rounds 37 and 39 of #294 were both this claim failing to reach a consumer — round 39's was in plugins/directives-toolkit/scripts/wait-gate.sh, whose PreToolUse message is the highest-authority copy of the rule because it is delivered unprompted at the decision point, and every .md-only sweep missed it. That carrier is listed here, and the pattern accepts 'arm a check-in' / 'arms a check-in' as well as 'arm the check-in' because the shell copy uses the indefinite article — an entry that named the round-39 file in its rationale while omitting it from its consumers, as the first draft of this one did, reproduces the exact failure it cites. The leading word boundary matters more here than in most patterns because this claim's exact INVERSION contains it: 'disarm a check-in' is the opposite instruction and the unanchored form certified it. A pattern that accepts the negation of its own claim is worse than no pattern, since it reports the regression as coverage — so the boundary is required in the per-consumer variant below as well. The negator lookbehind rejects 'never arm a check-in'. It deliberately checks only the word IMMEDIATELY before the verb: a clause-level negation scan was designed, measured and rejected, because ci-notify.yml legitimately reads 'a green run is not a guaranteed wake and a waiting session still arms a check-in', where the negator belongs to a different proposition in the same clause. 'never explicitly arm a check-in' therefore still passes; narrowing that needs the claim's CONDITION pinned, not just its verb.

consumers.why: This file states the rule TWICE — once in its explanatory header comment, once inside the echo the PreToolUse hook actually delivers. The claim-level pattern matched the header, so deleting the instruction from the DELIVERED message left the guard green on the copy that carries the most authority (it reaches a session unprompted, at the decision point). The pattern below requires the delivered message's own opening text, so only the emitted form satisfies it.
